item.title: An outbreak is beaten one house visit at a time
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Ebola reached an eighth Congolese province on Sunday. The headline counts provinces. The response counts tests, contacts and quiet health zones, and those are the numbers that end outbreaks.
item.content:encoded:
Ebola reached an eighth Congolese province on Sunday. The headline counts provinces. The response counts tests, contacts and quiet health zones, and those are the numbers that end outbreaks.

Congo’s health ministry said on Sunday that the Ebola outbreak had reached Nord-Ubangi, an eighth province, with two confirmed cases, one of them fatal, both men in their twenties1. Authorities have recorded at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, the deadliest in the country’s history. It is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment1. Reuters, citing the latest situation report, put the total at 9,415 cases and 4,536 deaths in the 24 hours to 16 October, with 67 new confirmed cases that day, 44 of them in Ituri3.

That is the headline, and it is grim. It is also the least useful number in the story. A province is a line on a map. An outbreak is beaten, or not, in smaller units: a sample in a laboratory, a contact visited at home, a burial done safely, a health zone that goes six weeks without a case.

Read the situation report, not the map. The ministry’s daily report for 14 October, published the next day, is a dull document in the best sense2. Laboratories analysed 506 samples, against 394 the day before, and the share testing positive fell to 12.8% from 17.3%2. More tests and a lower share of positives is the combination you want: it suggests the net is being cast wider, not that the virus is being found less because fewer people look. Of 4,048 alerts received, 98.5% had been verified, and every one of the 612 validated suspect cases had been investigated2.

Then the uncomfortable lines, printed just as plainly. Of 33,264 contacts to be followed, 25,956 were seen in the previous 24 hours: a follow-up rate of 78.0%, down from 81.8% the day before and below the required threshold of 95%2. Only 242 of the 612 suspects, 39.5%, had been transferred to transit or treatment centres2. Twenty-two of the day’s 37 confirmed deaths happened in the community rather than in a treatment centre2. And 269 front-line workers have been infected since the outbreak began2. Those are the gaps an outbreak travels through, and the report names them itself. A system that publishes its own shortfall every day is a system that can be held to fixing it.

Shrinking pockets, a wider map. The World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, Mohamed Yakub Janabi, put it in one sentence on Friday: “We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out”1. Both halves are in the data. Twelve of the 65 health zones touched so far had gone at least 42 days, two full incubation periods, without a new confirmed case, and three more were between 22 and 42 days2. Yet the newest provinces sit along the border with the Central African Republic, where armed violence has forced thousands to flee and roads and phone networks are poor1. Distance is the virus’s ally. Logistics is the response’s.

The authorities in North Kivu, where the WHO says substantial transmission continues1, are answering with logistics. From today, people coming from Ituri may not enter the province for a week. Motorcycles may carry only the driver and one passenger, taxis four. Burials are limited to 20 family members, and checkpoints must screen temperatures and provide hand-washing. Today is declared a “Stop Ebola Day”, with only authorised services at work4. None of this is glamorous. Most of it is enforceable. That is the point.

What was caught, and where. In Kenya an eighth case was confirmed on Sunday: a 49-year-old patient attendant, likely exposed to the country’s first case, who was tested after developing symptoms in quarantine. He was one of 38 people tested that day, and the six other living patients were stable5. A case found inside quarantine is the system working: the chain is visible and the contacts are already known. A case found in a market is the system being surprised. Kenya’s cases, so far, are the first kind.

Why this leads on a Monday in Berlin. Because the same lesson keeps arriving from different desks this morning. Oil is moving through a contested strait on escorts and detours rather than a treaty. A protest movement in France is being answered, or not, by a list of meetings and a payroll of substitute teachers. What decides the outcome is rarely the announcement. It is the follow-up.

Seventy-eight per cent is not good enough, by the response’s own standard. It is also a number, published daily, against a threshold, published daily. That is what accountability looks like before anyone holds a press conference about it. Watch it climb, or not. It will tell you more about this outbreak than the next province on the map.

Sources

  2. Rapport de situation de la 17e épidémie de la maladie à virus Ebola, SitRep N°153 (14 octobre 2026) — Ministère de la Santé Publique, Hygiène et Prévoyance Sociale, RDC
  3. DR Congo confirms Ebola outbreak has spread to eighth province — Reuters, via GMA News Online
  4. Ebola in North Kivu: Borders closed to travellers from Ituri for one week — Agence Congolaise de Presse (ACP)

item.title: Asia sold Friday at the open. The week will be settled by invoices.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Tokyo and Seoul paid for Wall Street's chip selling, oil gave a little back, and China beat its poll. The real calendar this week is more than seventy American company reports.
item.content:encoded:
Tokyo and Seoul paid for Wall Street's chip selling, oil gave a little back, and China beat its poll. The real calendar this week is more than seventy American company reports.

Asia took Friday’s American selling into Monday. Early in the session Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 2.15% and the broader Topix 1.17%; South Korea’s Kospi had lost 1.60%1. On Friday the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had slumped 3.8%1. US stock futures leaned the other way, with S&P 500 contracts up 0.2% and Nasdaq 100 contracts up 0.5%1.

Oil helped. Brent fell $1.94, or 1.77%, to $107.92 a barrel by 02:27 GMT, after settling on Friday at its highest since 19 May; WTI was at $100.582. The push came from Washington’s waiver of new Russia sanctions and tariffs, which may mean more Russian fuel on the market2. This edition’s Annex reads the order itself.

China’s third-quarter numbers beat the poll: growth of 4.5% on a year, against a 4.4% Reuters consensus and 4.3% in the second quarter3. The composition matters more than the beat. Growth leaned on factories and exports, while fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% in the first nine months and September retail sales rose just 1.1%3.

The week’s real calendar is corporate. More than 70 S&P 500 companies report, Tesla and Meta among them1. Netflix is due on Tuesday; Meta, Tesla, Lam Research and Texas Instruments on Wednesday4. After a week in which chip shares were priced on doubts about whether AI spending will earn its keep1, this is the first fresh evidence: revenue, capital spending and cash flow, printed by the companies themselves.

That is the constructive way to read a red Monday. Moods are cheap and fast. Invoices are slow and audited, and this week a great many of them arrive at once.

item.title: The Annex: what the Russia waiver actually waives
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The headline says sanctions were lifted. The order says the duties were written, set at 500% and 100%, and switched off in the same document, with the older sanctions left standing.
item.content:encoded:
The headline says sanctions were lifted. The order says the duties were written, set at 500% and 100%, and switched off in the same document, with the older sanctions left standing.

The annex this morning is the order itself, published by the White House on 16 October1. It is shorter than the commentary about it, and more precise.

Section 2 sets the duties. Goods from Russia: duty raised by 500% ad valorem. Goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude and gas, if they knowingly make new purchases on or after 18 October: plus 100%. Goods from the five largest facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion: plus 100%1.

Section 4 switches them off. Under section 115 of the act, the president waives “any duties” under sections 112 and 113, and the sanctions in a long list of other sections, having certified to Congress that the waiver is in the national interest1. The waivers “remain in effect until” the president or the secretary of state decides that further action is appropriate1. There is no end date. The waiver came two days before the law’s implementation deadline3.

What survives. “For the avoidance of doubt”, nothing in the order affects sanctions under the executive orders behind the national emergency on Russia, as continued on 24 March 20261. The older architecture stands; the new floor was built and not walked on. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president would take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact2.

What it sits next to. A diesel deal: Russian exports to the United States and others starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month and rising to about 7.6 million barrels a month, according to Trump’s announcement as reported by Reuters2. It follows a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 20273. On Sunday the president wrote that he could sign the sanctions “later, or any time that I want!”4. Zelenskyy called the waiver “wrong”3.

The reading. A law with a waiver clause is still a law. The duties exist on paper, the monitoring duty in section 3 exists, and section 5 names which department would pull which lever1. That is leverage stored, not leverage spent. Whether it is ever spent is a political question. Where it sits, and who holds the switch, is now a matter of public record, which is more than most podium lines leave behind.

  3. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as ‘wrong’ — CNBC

item.title: France answers a riot with a list of meetings, and that is not a joke
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Nearly 2,400 arrests, burned town halls, a presidential address. The part that will matter by Christmas is smaller: substitute teachers, a round table with a date, an after-action report.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 2,400 arrests, burned town halls, a presidential address. The part that will matter by Christmas is smaller: substitute teachers, a round table with a date, an after-action report.

Saturday was one of the most violent days of unrest France has seen in years. The interior ministry counted nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven seriously; in Paris alone police reported a record 855 arrests1. Town halls were stormed in Limoges, where the 19th-century building burned, in Marseille and in Lille, and traders’ unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked1.

On Sunday at 8pm Emmanuel Macron addressed the country2. He drew a hard line between the “plusieurs centaines de milliers”, several hundred thousand people, who marched with legitimate worries about the cost of living, fuel prices and schools, and those who “destroy, ransack and loot”1,2. Then he set out a method in three parts2. Prefects, with mayors, may ban certain gatherings. Parties and unions are asked to condemn violence without ambiguity. And this week the prime minister will bring pupils, students, teachers, unions, employers, local authorities and parliamentarians to one table to work on concrete proposals. The education ministry’s consultation platform has collected more than 100,000 contributions2. Macron also said he would travel to the Gulf states to secure fuel and gas supplies2.

Cynics will call a meeting a non-answer. The small print says otherwise. The government has already promised 3,000 more substitute teachers, a place for students in school decision-making, and has scrapped planned increases in some university registration fees3. That is the protesters’ original complaint, missing teachers and crumbling classrooms, answered in payroll lines rather than adjectives. The school protests began in late September, a week into the school year3, and they asked for staff, not slogans.

The harder question is the state’s own competence. The mayor of Limoges said his municipal police ran out of ammunition at about 3.30pm and called it “a colossal failure of the state”; politicians on the left and the right called for the interior minister’s resignation1. Macron asked the government to draw every lesson on intelligence and anticipation and promised full transparency2. That is a promise with a deliverable, an after-action report, and it should be held to one.

The constructive part is the calendar. France votes for a new president in April 20273, and Macron’s own framing on Sunday was that the argument belongs in public meetings, newspapers and peaceful rallies, not in the street2. Institutions that answer peaceful demands with budget lines and violent ones with courts are doing their job, slowly and without applause. This week’s test is simple: does the round table produce a number, with a date attached?

Sources

  1. Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France — The Guardian
  2. Adresse aux Français — Élysée
  3. Why are people protesting across Europe? — The Guardian

item.title: The picture is the minority. The march was the majority.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Your feed showed fire. The counts show several hundred thousand people walking. Before you form a view of a weekend, ask for the denominator.
item.content:encoded:
Your feed showed fire. The counts show several hundred thousand people walking. Before you form a view of a weekend, ask for the denominator.

Your feed this weekend showed fire: burning barricades in Paris, a torched town hall in Limoges, a wrecked carabinieri car in Milan2,3. Those images are real. They are also a biased sample, and the bias runs in a predictable direction.

By the French president’s own count, several hundred thousand people demonstrated on Saturday with legitimate demands1. The Guardian describes tens of thousands of peaceful marchers in major cities, parents, teachers and grandparents among them, separate from the groups that surprised the police and from the looters who followed2. Nearly 2,400 arrests is a large number. Set against several hundred thousand marchers, it is a small share. The camera, though, goes where the fire is.

Psychologists call this the availability heuristic: what comes to mind easily feels common. A burning building is easy to remember; a peaceful march of grandparents is not. The result is that a weekend gets remembered by its worst hour, and a cause gets judged by its worst participants.

The useful habit is the denominator. Lyon’s mayor, Grégory Doucet, asked for a “sense of nuance” and for “avoiding stereotypes”2. Milan’s mayor, Giuseppe Sala, called the reasons for the protest “understandable” and the violence “not justifiable”3. Both are denominator sentences: they keep the many and the few in separate columns.

Leaders know the bias, and lean on it in both directions. Portugal’s prime minister warned rivals against “importing” climates of instability that, he said, “have no support in Portuguese society”, while hundreds camped in Lisbon’s Rossio Square over rents3. Both can be true at once. The camp is small. The housing numbers behind it are not.

  2. Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France — The Guardian

item.title: Podium vs Print: “open for business” in the busiest week for attacks
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The admiral says the strait is open. The monitor counted ten ships attacked in a week. Both are true, and the second one is the one your fuel bill hears.
item.content:encoded:
The admiral says the strait is open. The monitor counted ten ships attacked in a week. Both are true, and the second one is the one your fuel bill hears.

The podium. In a video statement on Friday, Adm. Brad Cooper said about 400 merchant ships had sailed through the Strait of Hormuz in the previous seven days, and that US forces had helped Gulf partners ship more than 100 million barrels of crude in that period1. That brought the crude moved with US help in recent months to more than 1.3 billion barrels, he said. “Let me be clear,” he added: the strait “remains open for business”1.

The print. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency counted at least 10 vessels attacked in or near the strait since the previous Sunday, a weekly high since the war began in February, and 23 attacks since the start of October, almost double the average2. It also said it was “struggling to accurately report” the true number, because most ships now refuse to report attacks2. The analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday that intensified attacks had cut Gulf crude flows to about 8.5 million barrels a day on a seven-day average last week, from more than 20 million the week before3.

The gap. Desk arithmetic: 100 million barrels in seven days is about 14.3 million barrels a day. That is well above Kpler’s 8.5 million, but the two figures come from different counters, with different definitions and slightly different weeks, so do not subtract one from the other. Read them together instead. Ships are moving, in large numbers, and they are moving under fire. Many now switch off their tracking systems to avoid detection, and still face attacks2.

Verdict. Not a lie and not the whole truth. “Open” is a word about access. Price is a word about risk. A strait you can cross only with escorts and dark transponders is open the way a road with checkpoints is open: you get through, at a cost. That cost reaches you in delivered fuel prices long before it reaches a podium. It is also worth noticing what moved Brent this morning: a sanctions waiver in Washington, not a change at sea3.

  2. Live Updates: Iran says Strait of Hormuz reopening, seven-day ceasefire conditions still on the table — CBS News
  3. Oil tumbles as Trump’s Russia sanctions waiver may lead to more fuel supplies — Reuters, via Investing.com

item.title: A blackout week belongs to the prints
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Fed has gone quiet before its 28 October decision. That leaves the floor to inflation in London and Tokyo, surveys in Europe and a rate decision in Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed has gone quiet before its 28 October decision. That leaves the floor to inflation in London and Tokyo, surveys in Europe and a rate decision in Beijing.

The Federal Reserve has entered its communications blackout ahead of its 28 October decision1. For a week the most-quoted committee in the world says nothing in public, and that is a feature, not a gap. When the speakers go quiet, the data has the floor.

There is plenty of it. UK inflation for September arrives on Wednesday, after 3.1% in August; markets had priced a 95% chance that the Bank of England raises rates on 5 November, CMC Markets wrote on Friday2. The People’s Bank of China sets its lending rates on Tuesday, euro-area consumer confidence comes on Thursday, and on Friday the euro-area purchasing managers’ surveys and Japan’s September inflation2. CMC also notes that markets expect the Fed itself to raise rates sooner than the Bank of England, after hotter-than-expected September consumer and producer prices in the United States2.

Beijing is the quiet exception. Economists largely expect the People’s Bank to hold its benchmark lending rates through the rest of the year and leave the work to fiscal measures, such as the 550 billion yuan of unused debt quota passed to local governments in early October3.

Currencies are waiting too. The yen barely moved this morning at 157.89 per dollar, and the offshore yuan held at 6.68391.

The desk’s view is old-fashioned. A committee that talks every day trains markets to trade adjectives. A blackout sends everyone back to the invoice: what prices actually did last month, measured by statisticians who do not give interviews. You can do the same this week. Skip the previews. Read the releases.

item.title: Ordinary Ledger: heating oil is the one bill with a delivery date
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Gas and power arrive smoothed, by the month. Heating oil arrives by lorry, once a year, at the price of the day. This October that price has been falling while the pump has not.
item.content:encoded:
Gas and power arrive smoothed, by the month. Heating oil arrives by lorry, once a year, at the price of the day. This October that price has been falling while the pump has not.

If your home is heated with oil, your heating bill works differently from your neighbour’s. Gas and electricity arrive by the month, smoothed and averaged. Heating oil arrives by lorry, once or twice a year, and the price on the day of the order is the price of the winter.

That price, by the national average the comparison portal tanke-günstig publishes for a 2,000-litre order, was €177.59 per 100 litres late on Sunday1. The spread between the Länder is wide: €171.90 in Saxony-Anhalt, €183.91 in Hesse, €174.90 in Berlin1. On Friday the portal noted that heating oil had fallen by almost ten cents a litre since the start of October, unlike motor fuels1. ADAC’s last weekly reading still had diesel at €2.247 a litre2.

Part of the bill is not set by the market at all. The portal estimates that taxes made up about 40% of the end price in 2025, with the CO₂ levy alone at about 17.7%, more than the energy tax itself1. That part is known in advance and changes by law, on a date, which makes it the most predictable line on the invoice.

The ordinary lesson is not “order now”. This desk does not give that advice, and nobody can time a war. It is that a once-a-year bill rewards knowing your own numbers: tank size, last winter’s litres, what you paid per 100 litres. The household arithmetic for a typical order is in “In euros at home” at the end of this edition.

And a word for the dull machinery. The depot schedulers, drivers and invoicing clerks who get a full tank into a cellar in Hesse in a month like this one are among the least celebrated parts of Europe’s energy system. They are also a part that works.

item.title: Chip shares fell. The bond prices say why.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The AI sell-off is usually told as a story about mood. Told in bond prices, it is a story about the cost of the loan that builds the data centre.
item.content:encoded:
The AI sell-off is usually told as a story about mood. Told in bond prices, it is a story about the cost of the loan that builds the data centre.

Friday’s selling in chipmakers, which took the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 3.8%2, is usually told as a story about mood. The more useful version is told in bond prices.

CoreWeave’s most-traded bonds, paying 9.75% and due in 2031, traded as low as 78 cents on the dollar on 14 October, a yield of 16.39%, having started October at about 851. Its 9.625% bonds due 2032 slumped to 75, for a 16.5% yield, against 103.625 on 2 June1. Both recovered some ground the next day, to 83 and 801. In the same week the data-centre developer Cipher Digital announced an $850 million offering of zero-coupon convertible notes, and JPMorgan analysts cut Applied Digital’s project bonds to neutral, citing a looming “supply overhang” of debt still to be raised1.

That is the mechanism. Much of the AI build-out is financed by lenders who expect to be paid back in fixed instalments. When the price of that debt rises, the cost of every future data centre rises with it, and the shares of companies selling into those data centres get marked down in sympathy. It is not a verdict on the technology. It is a repricing of the loan.

The same report carries the counter-signal. CleanSpark’s bonds held up better, helped by good news from its client Meta, after investors read early retention data for Meta’s Muse assistant as evidence that the company can earn money on its AI spending1. Meta reports on Wednesday, alongside Tesla, Lam Research and Texas Instruments3.

Those reports are the invoices. Read three lines: capital spending, cash flow, and who is paying whom. The rest is the podium.

item.title: An energy ceasefire that nobody is counting at zero
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Kyiv counts 76 Russian strikes on its energy system since the announcement. Moscow counts 1,015 Ukrainian drones in a day. A ceasefire without a neutral ledger is a podium.
item.content:encoded:
Kyiv counts 76 Russian strikes on its energy system since the announcement. Moscow counts 1,015 Ukrainian drones in a day. A ceasefire without a neutral ledger is a podium.

On 11 October President Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, without giving details1. A week later both sides are publishing counts, and neither count is zero.

Zelenskyy wrote on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since the announcement, that facilities in four regions had been struck overnight, and that tens of thousands of families were without power1. Kyiv had initially said it was observing the ceasefire, then resumed strikes on Russian oil facilities on Thursday after a three-day pause1. On Sunday Russia’s defence ministry said it had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea. In St Petersburg the oil terminal and the Ruchi oil depot caught fire; one person was killed and five wounded, the regional governor said1.

Diplomacy runs alongside. Zelenskyy said US-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time”, and that he had spoken with the envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about next steps1. Trump, defending his sanctions waiver, wrote that he did not want to drive Russia “away from the bargaining table” and that “great progress is being made”1,2.

The desk’s view: a ceasefire without a verification mechanism is a podium. It becomes a print when someone neutral starts counting. What would make this one real is dull to the point of tedium: an agreed list of covered facilities, a start time, a reporting channel and a third party that logs incidents and publishes them. None of that has been made public.

Until it is, read both numbers, 76 and 1,015, for what they are. They are not evidence that a ceasefire failed. They are evidence that one has not yet been built. Ceasefires that hold are almost always the boring kind, with an annex.

item.title: Adam: the warning is the infrastructure
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Spain's storm reached its worst hours on Sunday, with red warnings on the Valencia and Alicante coast. The rain is weather. A warning that arrives in time and is followed is policy.
item.content:encoded:
Spain's storm reached its worst hours on Sunday, with red warnings on the Valencia and Alicante coast. The rain is weather. A warning that arrives in time and is followed is policy.

The storm Spain calls dana Adam, a cut-off low, entered its most adverse phase on Sunday, and the state weather agency AEMET expected it to last into Monday1. AEMET kept a red warning, its highest level, on the coast of southern Valencia province and northern Alicante, for 90 litres per square metre in an hour and accumulations of 200 litres in 12 hours and 300 in 241. The Balearics were lowered to orange on Sunday afternoon; Andalusia and Murcia stayed on orange1.

The gauges were already filling. On Sunday AEMET’s stations recorded 149.6 litres per square metre in Miramar, 135.4 in Pego and 131.7 in Oliva, and the regional association Avamet measured almost 250 litres in Barx by 18:501. On Saturday a woman in Cabrera de Mar, north of Barcelona, was swept away while crossing a flooded street with her family; her body was found on Sunday1. AEMET warned that much of the rain is falling on ground that is already saturated1.

There is a temperature story underneath. Before the cold front arrived on Saturday, temperatures across the northern half of the peninsula had been about ten degrees above normal; by Sunday they were back to normal or slightly below1.

Valencia has reason to know that the most important part of a storm is the instruction attached to it. AEMET’s spokesman, Rubén del Campo, called it “fundamental” to follow the civil-protection advice and not to travel unless strictly necessary1. A red warning is only infrastructure if it arrives in time, is believed and is acted on. That chain, forecaster to phone to person, is now being tested on the Safor coast.

The constructive part is that the chain exists, is public and is specific: litres per hour, named coasts, named hours. AEMET expects the instability to ease from Tuesday1. The second test comes then, in the claims and the clean-up, and it is just as dull and just as important.

item.title: The Sunday Sequence: the week, in the order it reached the kitchen
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The barrel moved first, the pump second, the stockpile third, the committees fourth and the podium last. The household pays at step two and is consulted at step five.
item.content:encoded:
The barrel moved first, the pump second, the stockpile third, the committees fourth and the podium last. The household pays at step two and is consulted at step five.

On Sundays the desk rearranges the week. Not by the size of the headline, but in the order the incentives actually moved: barrels, pumps, stockpiles, committees, podiums. The order matters more than any single number in it, because the order tells you who pays first and who speaks last.

1. The barrel moved first. By ADAC’s count, Brent closed on Tuesday at about $106 a barrel, up from a little over $100 the week before1. On Friday December Brent settled at $109.86, up 3.72% on the day and its highest close since mid-May; WTI rose 3.55% to $101.41, its first close above $100 in nearly a month2. Both had traded lower earlier in the session2. On Friday morning this desk wrote that the futures screen was pricing a calmer future than the physical tank. By the close the screen had walked some of the way towards the tank. That is what a gap closing from below looks like, and it is not the comfortable direction.

2. The pump moved second. ADAC’s weekly reading put diesel at €2.247 a litre, up 1.4 cents on the week, and Super E10 at €2.151, up 2.5 cents1. That is with the fuel-tax cut in place: since 1 October the energy tax on petrol and diesel is 14 cents lower, which ADAC puts at just under 17 cents a litre including VAT, until the end of December1. Relief is real. It is simply measured against a price you never get to see.

3. The stockpile moved third. On Thursday the International Energy Agency agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel, with wholesale diesel above $200 a barrel in Singapore and around $220 in Europe and the US2. In the same week the agency said exports out of the Middle East had recovered to pre-crisis levels and that global oil storage was not tight, while also warning that the diesel shortage would persist well into next year2. Both statements can be true. Crude finds detours. Diesel has to be made, and a refinery is a factory, not a pipe.

4. The committees spoke fourth. In Bangkok on Friday, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, declined to signal anything: “I don’t prejudge meetings”3. On Saturday Christine Lagarde told the IMF’s steering committee that the energy shock is “too large to ‘look through’”, but that “a measured response remains appropriate”, and that wages have so far shown no material response4. Committees speak after prices on purpose. They are paid to wait for the second print, wages, not the first one, the barrel.

5. The podium came last. On Saturday Iran’s foreign minister said Tehran had sent Washington, through Qatar, a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if its conditions were met. “The choice is now America’s,” he said5. The markets were closed. The first price to answer will be Monday’s, and it will answer in dollars, not adjectives.

Where the household sits. Between step two and step four. You pay at the pump before any committee has decided whether the pump matters. Eurostat’s September figures show the split inside one house: liquid and motor fuels up 33.8% on a year across the euro area, electricity, gas and heat up 6.9%, core inflation near 2.5%7. The pipe that comes into your house decides your month more than the average does. That is not a scandal; it is the design. A central bank that moved on every barrel would be a weather vane, and weather vanes are poor at keeping prices stable.

The constructive half. The same order works in reverse. Relief, when it comes, travels the same road: barrel first, pump after, committee later, podium claiming credit at the end. You do not need to guess when. You only need to know which number to watch first, and it is never the speech.

The Friday calls, scored. A desk that makes calls should keep the receipts.

  • “The screen is the forecast. The tank is the invoice.” Open. Futures rose towards spot by Friday’s close2, but the spot price for that day is not yet published. We will score it after the EIA release.
  • “The average stock had a better day than the index” (Thursday). Not repeated. On Friday slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, and the index lost 1.1%6. It was a day, not a regime, and we said so too quietly.
  • “The committee is behind the print, on purpose.” Holding. Saturday’s statement says so in the committee’s own words: no evidence yet of significant pass-through to other prices and wages beyond what was already projected4.

None of this is advice. It is an order of events, and the order is the most honest thing the week produced.

item.title: The worst week since June, from a record nine trading days old
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A 2% drawdown is a mood. Who fell, and who did not, is the information.
item.content:encoded:
A 2% drawdown is a mood. Who fell, and who did not, is the information.

The S&P 500 fell 1.95% on the week to 7,659.44, its largest weekly percentage fall since the week ending 26 June, according to Dow Jones Market Data1. Friday alone took 1.09%. The index is now 2.04% below the record close of 7,818.93 set on Tuesday, 6 October, and has fallen on six of the last eight trading days1.

Keep the scale in view. The same data show the index still up 11.89% this year and 11.35% since the war began on 28 February1. A record nine trading days old is not a crash; it is a high-water mark the market has stepped back from.

The composition is the story. The Nasdaq Composite lost 4.5% on the week, while the Dow industrials still rose2. The Wall Street Journal put CoreWeave at the centre of the week’s tech rout, with investors worried about what higher borrowing costs do to the most leveraged players in the data-centre build-out2. Friday’s damage was broad but not total: slightly more than half of S&P 500 stocks fell3.

So money did not leave the market. It moved from the companies that need financing towards the ones that send invoices and collect them. That is the dull machinery working: a rising cost of money sorting balance sheets, one bond yield at a time.

item.title: Podium vs Print: a seven-day plan and a detour already running
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A plan with a date in it is better than a plan without one. The ships, meanwhile, are already working around the strait.
item.content:encoded:
A plan with a date in it is better than a plan without one. The ships, meanwhile, are already working around the strait.

The podium, in its own words. On Saturday Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had sent Washington, through Qatar, “a specific seven-day plan”: if Iran’s conditions are met, the strait can reopen and normal traffic resume within seven days. “The choice is now America’s,” he said1. He also said US military action had prevented implementation of the June memorandum of understanding1. An Iranian lawmaker told local media that indirect talks were continuing through Qatar and Oman, and that both sides had exchanged conditions3.

The print. The market has not been waiting. Gulf producers have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast: Vortexa counted 82 ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Kutch last month, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, roughly two-thirds of it refined products2. The IEA says exports out of the Middle East have recovered to pre-crisis levels through this makeshift network, even as it buckles under congestion and attacks2.

The gap. The plan has a date in it, which is more than most speeches offer, and dates bind in a way adjectives do not. But its conditions were not published, and a deadline whose terms you cannot read is only half a sentence. The detour, by contrast, is fully legible: it has a location, a count and a volume.

Verdict. Not a contradiction, a sequence. The podium describes a door; the print describes people already climbing through a window. If the door opens, the window gets quieter and cheaper. Until then, the window is the supply chain, and it is more expensive than a door.

item.title: Resilience doesn't fall from the sky. It is filed.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The IMF's Bangkok meetings closed with a sentence worth framing, and a warning about standing on one leg.
item.content:encoded:
The IMF's Bangkok meetings closed with a sentence worth framing, and a warning about standing on one leg.

The IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings closed in Bangkok on Saturday. The chair’s statement opened with a line that suits this desk: the global economy “has weathered the latest in a series of shocks better than expected, but continued resilience should not be taken for granted”2.

Kristalina Georgieva’s summary was sharper. Members recognised that investment in good policies and institutions has anchored the global economy: “resilience doesn’t fall from the sky”1. She also warned that relying on the AI boom as the main source of support is a risk, “like we stand on one leg”1.

Her second point was divergence. Energy-importing countries that are not part of the AI value chain are “falling further behind”, and from a position of vulnerability to begin with1. The committee’s chair, Saudi finance minister Mohammed Aljadaan, asked fiscal authorities for credible medium-term plans to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable people and growth-enhancing investment3.

None of that will move a market on Monday. It is not meant to. A communiqué is a to-do list that finance ministries take home, and the constructive part is that the list is boring: buffers, debt plans, supervision. Boring lists, kept, are how the last shock was weathered.

item.title: The present feels worse than the future, which is the oil market's mood too
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: American consumers marked today down sharply and tomorrow up slightly. The screen and the tank, again, in survey form.
item.content:encoded:
American consumers marked today down sharply and tomorrow up slightly. The screen and the tank, again, in survey form.

The University of Michigan’s preliminary October survey put consumer sentiment at 46.3, down from 48.1 in September and 53.6 a year ago1. That headline hides a split worth naming.

Current economic conditions fell 12.2% in a month, to 44.7. Consumer expectations rose 2.2%, to 47.31. People rate today worse and the months ahead slightly better. It is the same shape as this week’s oil market: an expensive present and a hoped-for calmer future.

The survey’s director, Joanne Hsu, said buying conditions for durable goods “plummeted amid high prices and borrowing costs”, and that sentiment fell steeply among lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios, the groups with fewer resources to absorb price rises1.

The figure committees will read twice is inflation expectations: 4.7% for the year ahead and 3.5% for the long run, both the highest since May1. Expectations are a behaviour, not a feeling. People who expect prices to rise ask for raises and buy early, which is why central banks guard this number more carefully than any podium line. The constructive read: the long-run number rose by a tenth of a point in a month, from 3.4% to 3.5%1, not by a full point. The public is pricing a shock, and not yet a spiral. That is a sensible public.

item.title: Three-quarters full is a European number. Germany's is three-fifths.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: EU gas storage enters winter at 74%. The average is a comfort; the spread between countries is the work.
item.content:encoded:
EU gas storage enters winter at 74%. The average is a comfort; the spread between countries is the work.

EU gas storage was 74.3% full on 16 October, about 842 TWh, according to GIE’s AGSI+ data as compiled by GasRadar1. GIE’s platform reports daily for every underground store in the EU2. That is the number that will be quoted all winter.

Look under it. On the same data Italy was 89.5% full and France 87.4%, while Germany stood at 60.7%1. A comfortable-looking average can sit on top of a thin national number, and a thinner store means leaning harder on daily imports through the winter. European LNG terminals sent out about 3,610 GWh a day on 16 October1: ships, not caverns, are the margin this winter.

On the oil side, the IEA said this week that the diesel shortage triggered by the war would persist well into next year3. Gas and diesel are different molecules with the same lesson: a stock is a buffer you build in summer and spend in winter, and the bill for a thin buffer arrives as a price, not as a shortage.

The constructive part is that this is the most transparent energy system Europe has ever run. Every store reports daily, in public, for free. You can watch the winter being spent one gas day at a time, which is more than any podium will tell you.

item.title: No free riders: the committees are tightening together
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Warsh would not pre-announce. Lagarde would not look through. Both told you how they decide, which is more useful than what they will decide.
item.content:encoded:
Warsh would not pre-announce. Lagarde would not look through. Both told you how they decide, which is more useful than what they will decide.

Kevin Warsh used a fireside chat in Bangkok to decline the one thing markets wanted. “I don’t prejudge meetings,” the Fed chair said, adding that forward guidance is a business the Fed is “not in … anymore”1. He described “a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world”, which means “there’s no free riders”1. The Fed raised its range to 3.75–4% last month; CME FedWatch showed traders pricing a 72.3% chance of no change at the 27–28 October meeting1.

Christine Lagarde’s statement to the IMF’s steering committee was the European version, in writing. The ECB raised rates by 25 basis points in June and again in September2. Headline inflation was 3.8% in September and core 2.5%, and wages “have so far shown no material response to the energy shock”2. Financing conditions have tightened, with long-term rates rising notably, which “will slow growth and reduce pass-through” more than projected in September2.

Read the two together and the method is the message. Both central banks are saying: the bond market has already done some of our work, wages have not yet moved, so we will look at the data rather than at you. The ECB’s next decision comes on 29 October, after a two-day meeting in Frankfurt3.

For you, the useful part is that this is not a mystery. The ECB publishes its three criteria: the inflation outlook, underlying inflation, and how strongly policy is getting through2. Watch those three and you will not need the podium.

item.title: A backlog is a promise. Cash flow is the invoice.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: CoreWeave's default insurance hit distress levels while its order book sat above $100 billion. Both numbers are true; the bond market chose which one to price.
item.content:encoded:
CoreWeave's default insurance hit distress levels while its order book sat above $100 billion. Both numbers are true; the bond market chose which one to price.

This week the AI build-out met its oldest constraint: the cost of waiting to be paid. CoreWeave, a so-called neocloud that rents out computing power, has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to fund its build-out1. On Thursday the yield on its 9.75% bond due 2031 reached 15.78%, and the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, insurance against default, briefly went above 1,140 basis points before settling near 1,0381. S&P Global Market Intelligence’s Gavan Nolan said a spread of 1,000 basis points or more is generally a sign of credit distress1.

The counter-argument is a big number. The company’s backlog is over $100 billion, about two-thirds of it with investment-grade customers, Deutsche Bank said1. Nolan’s point was that no one doubts the demand; “the question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive”1. A backlog is a promise to pay later. A bond coupon is due on a date.

The stress travelled. Oracle’s five-year spread rose about 10% on the week, to around 282 basis points1, and the Journal said investors were fretting over how higher borrowing costs hit the most leveraged players in the data-centre build-out2.

The constructive read: this is markets doing their job early. Pricing financing risk while the chips are still in demand is far cheaper than discovering it after the build-out. The machines are real; the invoices will decide who owns them.

item.title: Ebola readiness is a checklist, and checklists work
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: No cases in the WHO's eastern Mediterranean region, and 22 countries preparing as if there might be. That is what prevention looks like from the outside: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
No cases in the WHO's eastern Mediterranean region, and 22 countries preparing as if there might be. That is what prevention looks like from the outside: nothing.

The World Health Organization is stepping up Ebola preparedness across its eastern Mediterranean region, 22 countries and territories spanning parts of Africa, Asia and Europe, with priority support for Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan1. It follows deadly outbreaks caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, and a confirmed case in Kenya linked to the DRC1.

There have been no Ebola cases in the region so far1. Between July and September WHO sent missions to the three priority countries to test surveillance, laboratories, infection control, case management and emergency coordination, and it is closing gaps with training, supplies and simulation exercises1.

The hard part is honest in the text: gaps remain in early detection, lab confirmation and protective equipment, and conflict and restricted access make everything harder in countries already in humanitarian emergency1. WHO’s Director-General, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, called the region “the epicentre of global humanitarian need” this week1.

This is the desk’s favourite kind of health story, because it is all machinery: checklists, contingency plans, traveller guidance, a simulation run before the real thing. It does not make headlines when it works, and that is the point.

item.title: An energy ceasefire is measured in distillation units
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A pause announced on 11 October lasted four days. The way to read it is not by the statements but by which units are running.
item.content:encoded:
A pause announced on 11 October lasted four days. The way to read it is not by the statements but by which units are running.

On 11 October the US president announced an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kyiv. Ukraine paused refinery strikes, then lifted the pause on 15 October, President Zelensky said, citing continued Russian attacks on Ukraine’s grid1. That same day a drone attack hit Russia’s Ryazan refinery, and one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, stopped, Reuters reported, citing industry sources1.

The detail is in the unit numbers. CDU-6 had already been shut after a strike in September; the refinery’s three other primary units, CDU-1, CDU-3 and CDU-4, reportedly keep running1. The plant was also hit on 6 September and 15 May, and repairs after May lasted until around mid-July1. On 16 October, Zelensky said, Russia launched one of its largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, targeting more than 15 key facilities1.

This matters beyond the front line because diesel is the tightest part of the oil market. Days earlier Washington had lifted sanctions so Russia could supply diesel to global markets2, and a refinery under drone attack produces less of it, whatever is promised for export.

A second front runs through Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport 20 times in October, and Saudi officials say at least 19 people have been killed in recent attacks across the kingdom3. Keeping the night boring is now a job done on two seas and one long front, and it is done by crews, not by statements.

item.title: A storm called Adam is a water budget with a deadline
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Spain's first high-impact cut-off low of the season peaks today and tomorrow. The forecasts are written in litres per square metre, which is how a river sends its invoice.
item.content:encoded:
Spain's first high-impact cut-off low of the season peaks today and tomorrow. The forecasts are written in litres per square metre, which is how a river sends its invoice.

Spain’s civil protection authority, working from the state weather agency AEMET’s forecasts, has kept an alert in place for very strong and persistent showers and thunderstorms along the Mediterranean coast and the Balearic Islands from Saturday to at least Monday, the first high-impact dana, an isolated upper-level low, of the season1. Sunday and Monday are expected to be the worst days1.

The numbers are written as water, not wind. Around Cabo de La Nao and the Pitiusas, Ibiza and Formentera, more than 150 litres per square metre could fall in 12 hours, with 80 litres possible along the coasts of Alicante, Murcia and eastern Catalonia; over the whole episode local totals of 150 to 300 litres are possible1. Soils already saturated by earlier rain raise the risk of flash floods in streams and ramblas, the dry riverbeds that fill in hours1.

It follows several days of temperatures that AEMET called anomalously high for the time of year; a cold front is due to bring them back to normal or slightly below1. Heat, then a deluge, then a chill: the season’s three invoices in one weekend.

The constructive part sits in the same document. It is a plain, public list of what to do: do not drive through flooded stretches, do not park in flood-prone spots, move essentials upstairs if you have to leave1. Warnings like this, issued two days ahead, are one of the most cost-effective things a state does.

item.title: A president removed, a barrel unimpressed
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Venezuela changed hands over a weekend. The oil market read the supply sheet and went back to its glut. It was right about Venezuela, and about nothing that came next.
item.content:encoded:
Venezuela changed hands over a weekend. The oil market read the supply sheet and went back to its glut. It was right about Venezuela, and about nothing that came next.

On Saturday 3 January the United States captured Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro. A country holding the world’s largest proven oil reserves changed management over a weekend. On Monday, Brent futures settled $1.01 higher, at $61.76 a barrel1. That was the whole drama.

By Wednesday the price was lower than before the raid. Brent settled at $60.70 on Tuesday and $59.96 on Wednesday, as traders weighed an ample supply outlook and a deal, announced by President Trump, to import up to $2 billion worth of Venezuelan crude into the United States2,3. One broker, PVM’s Tamas Varga, put the market’s view in a sentence: “oil supply will be sufficient in 2026, with or without an increase in production from the OPEC member”2.

The market was right about Venezuela. Its exports averaged about 605,000 barrels a day in January, down from 780,000 in 2025, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters4. That is a loss you can measure, and a small one against a world that the International Energy Agency then expected to be oversupplied by 3.7 million barrels a day in 20264. Regime change is a political event. Supply is a logistics event. The screen only pays for the second.

January still had a move, just not that one. On the EIA’s spot series, Brent went from $61.35 on 31 December to $72.25 on 30 January, a rise of about 18% on the desk’s arithmetic5. Reuters’ Ron Bousso listed the causes at the time: a power outage that halted Kazakhstan’s giant Tengiz field on 18 January, a winter storm that cut US output by up to 2 million barrels a day, and President Trump’s increasingly explicit threats against Iran4. Even so, his column argued that the price was “stuck in a narrow band”, and that a break into triple digits “would likely need to be a doomsday scenario”4.

Hindsight, used honestly. The column was a fair reading of the evidence on 30 January. It was also, as it happened, a description of March. Four weeks later the United States and Israel struck Iran; by 31 March the same spot series read $126.695. There is no prize for pretending to have seen it coming, and this desk claims none. The lesson is narrower and more useful: the market had correctly learned to ignore noise, and the price of that discipline is that it ignores the signal too, until the signal sinks a tanker.

For you, the January record is a reminder about where to look. Not at who holds the palace, but at who holds the export terminal, the pipeline and the insurance certificate. The first changes the news. The others change the invoice.

item.title: The court sends the invoice back
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Six justices said a tariff is a tax, and taxes belong to Congress. The refund goes to whoever signed the customs entry, which is rarely the person who paid the higher price.
item.content:encoded:
Six justices said a tariff is a tax, and taxes belong to Congress. The refund goes to whoever signed the customs entry, which is rarely the person who paid the higher price.

On Friday 20 February the Supreme Court decided Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump by six votes to three2. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the majority, joined by Justices Barrett, Gorsuch, Jackson, Kagan and Sotomayor; Justice Kavanaugh wrote the principal dissent, joined by Justices Thomas and Alito1. The holding was short: the emergency-powers law the administration had used does not authorise the President to impose tariffs1.

The reasoning was shorter still. The power to “regulate… importation” is not the power to tax, and tariffs are a tax, which under the Constitution belongs to Congress. As the majority put it, “had Congress intended to convey the distinct and extraordinary power to impose tariffs, it would have done so expressly”1.

Institutions beat influencers, again. Within hours there was a replacement: a 10% tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, effective 24 February, capped by statute at 15% and at 150 days unless Congress extends it1. Markets took the day calmly; stocks rose and Treasury yields edged up, with investors estimating that the government might owe $150 billion to $200 billion in refunds3. The ruling did not decide refunds at all1.

The invoice tells you who paid. Customs duties are collected from importers, and the national accounts show how large the bill became. On the Bureau of Economic Analysis series, federal customs receipts ran at an annual rate of about $89 billion in the fourth quarter of 2024 and about $367 billion a year later5. That is the line in the chart below, and it is not an opinion about trade policy. It is a record of who sent money to the Treasury.

The refund follows the paperwork, not the price. Customs built a portal for IEEPA refunds, with interest4. Its own guidance is blunt: “CBP is only able to refund IEEPA duties to the Importer of Record” or a party that importer designates4. If a retailer passed the tariff on to you at the till, the refund goes to the retailer. That is not a scandal; it is how invoices work. It is also why “the tariff was struck down” and “you got your money back” are different sentences.

Hindsight. The series did not fall back to 2024 levels: receipts were still running at about $306 billion a year in the second quarter of 20265. Duties under other laws stayed in force, and the replacement levy took over part of the job1. The court changed who may decide. It did not change the habit of deciding.

item.title: The month a strait became a price
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Twenty million barrels a day stopped moving, and the world's emergency cupboard opened wider than ever before. Both facts were true. Only one of them was a solution.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty million barrels a day stopped moving, and the world's emergency cupboard opened wider than ever before. Both facts were true. Only one of them was a solution.

On 28 February the United States and Israel launched joint air strikes on Iran1. On 2 March Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and traffic fell to an average of about five vessels a day, against roughly a hundred before the war4. By the time the IEA published its March oil report on the 12th, flows of crude and products through the strait had gone “from around 20 mb/d before the war to a trickle”, and Gulf producers had cut output by at least 10 million barrels a day1. The agency called it “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”1.

The screen and the cargo. The physical price moved first and furthest. On the EIA’s spot series Brent was $71.32 on 27 February and $126.69 on 31 March, a rise of about 78% in a month on the desk’s arithmetic5. Futures were calmer: the IEA noted Brent futures had traded “within a whisker of $120” before easing to around $92 as it went to press1. Two prices, one barrel, and the gap between them was the cost of actually having the oil.

The cupboard opened. On 11 March all 32 IEA member countries agreed unanimously to make 400 million barrels of emergency stocks available2. It was the sixth collective action since the agency was founded in 1974, after 1991, 2005, 2011 and twice in 20222, and by the IEA’s own description “by far the largest ever”3. Members held more than 1.2 billion barrels of emergency stockpiles, plus 600 million barrels of industry stocks held under government obligation2.

Same units, please. Four hundred million barrels sounds like an answer. Measured against a disruption of nearly 20 million barrels a day1, it is about twenty days of the missing flow, on the desk’s arithmetic, released over months rather than days3. The IEA said as much, in calmer words: the release was “a significant and welcome buffer”, and the most important factor for stable flows was “the resumption of regular transit of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz”3.

Hindsight. March taught the year’s central lesson early. Stocks buy time; corridors decide prices. Every later month in this ledger is, in one way or another, a footnote to that sentence. If you run a business with a fuel bill, the useful question from March was never “how much is being released?” but “when do ships move again, and who insures them?”

item.title: A reference forecast is a hope with a footnote
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The IMF did not publish a baseline in April. It published a reference case and said, in plain print, that the world was drifting away from it. Read the footnote first.
item.content:encoded:
The IMF did not publish a baseline in April. It published a reference case and said, in plain print, that the world was drifting away from it. Read the footnote first.

April began with the year’s highest print and a ceasefire. On the EIA spot series Brent reached $138.21 on 7 April, the day the United States and Iran agreed a two-week ceasefire6, and fell to $122.11 the next day4. A week later, on 14 April, the IMF published its spring World Economic Outlook under the title Global Economy in the Shadow of War1.

The honest part was the format. The Fund did not call its central number a baseline. It called it a “reference forecast”, predicated on a war of “limited duration, intensity, and scope, such that the disruptions will fade by mid-2026”, consistent with futures prices as of 10 March1. On that basis world growth would be 3.1% in 2026, 0.2 percentage point lower than in January, with headline inflation rising to 4.4%1. Without the war, the Fund said, it would have revised growth up, to 3.4%2.

Then it printed the alternatives. In an adverse scenario, growth falls to 2.5% and inflation rises to 5.4%; in a severe one, where disruptions extend into 2027, growth falls to 2% this year and next and inflation exceeds 6%2. Reuters reported the same day that the world was “already drifting toward a more adverse scenario”, and that the reference case assumed oil averaging $82 a barrel in 2026, well below the futures price of about $963.

Why this matters for you. A reference forecast is not a prediction; it is a conditional sentence with the condition in small print. If your budget, your pay round or your mortgage plan borrowed the 3.1%, it also borrowed the assumption that the strait would reopen by summer. The useful reading of April was to price the condition, not the headline.

Hindsight. The condition failed; the number, curiously, held. In October the IMF still projected 3.1% for 2026, “broadly unchanged from April, despite a more persistent energy market disruption than anticipated”5. The economy bent around the shock through rerouting, inventories and an investment boom5. The footnote was wrong and the headline survived, which is the most dangerous kind of right: it teaches people to skip the footnote.

item.title: A new chair, the same arithmetic
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The Federal Reserve changed its chair in the middle of an energy shock. If you expected the new face to bring cheaper money, the committee's next four months are the answer.
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Reserve changed its chair in the middle of an energy shock. If you expected the new face to bring cheaper money, the committee's next four months are the answer.

On Friday 22 May Kevin Warsh took the oath of office as chairman of the Federal Reserve, and the Federal Open Market Committee unanimously chose him as its chair1. He had been nominated on 4 March and confirmed by the Senate as chairman on 13 May, by 54 votes to 451,2. Jerome Powell’s term as chair ended the same day; he had led the Board since 5 February 2018 and remains a governor, in a seat that runs to January 20283. For the week in between, the Board named him chair pro tempore, “consistent with past practice”4.

The ceremony was not the usual one. NBC News noted that the last Fed chair sworn in at the White House was Alan Greenspan, in 19875. If you read institutions by their rituals, that was the detail to notice. If you read them by their votes, it was not.

The votes. At the new chair’s first meeting, on 16–17 June, the committee held the federal funds target at 3.5% to 3.75% by twelve votes to none, in a statement that ended: “The Committee will deliver price stability”6. In July it held again, but three members, Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan, dissented because they wanted a quarter-point increase7. In September the committee raised the range to 3.75% to 4%, unanimously, saying the move “will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”8.

The arithmetic did not change with the chair. Inflation was, in the committee’s own words, “elevated relative to the Committee’s 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks… including energy”6. A chair can change the tone, the length of the statement and the setting of the oath. He cannot change what an oil shock does to a price index, or how eleven other voters read it.

Hindsight. Whatever you expected of the change at the top, the record from May to September is one of a committee tightening into a supply shock, not loosening around a personality. That is not a judgement on anyone’s independence. It is a reminder of where the decision sits: in a room with twelve votes and published minutes. Institutions beat influencers, including when the influencer holds the chair.

item.title: Frankfurt raises into a supply shock
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: The textbook says look through an energy shock. The ECB chose not to, for the first time in this cycle, and said exactly why. The interesting word was 'robust'.
item.content:encoded:
The textbook says look through an energy shock. The ECB chose not to, for the first time in this cycle, and said exactly why. The interesting word was 'robust'.

On 11 June the ECB’s Governing Council raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points, taking the deposit facility rate to 2.25% from 17 June1. It was the first increase since September 2023; the rate had been cut step by step to 2.00% by June 2025 and then left alone2.

The reason was stated, not implied. “The war in the Middle East is generating inflation pressures,” the statement said, “and the decision to raise rates is robust across a range of scenarios”1. Staff projected headline inflation at 3.0% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027 and 2.0% in 2028, with inflation excluding energy and food at 2.5% in 2026 and 20271. Growth was cut to 0.8% for 20261.

The textbook and the decision. The standard advice is that a central bank should look through a supply shock: higher oil prices are a one-off level change that tighter money cannot pump out of the ground. The ECB’s answer, read carefully, was about second-round effects. Staff expected the energy path “to some extent” to “feed into food, goods and services inflation”1. You do not raise rates to lower the price of diesel. You raise them so that the diesel price does not become next year’s wage claim and the year after’s rent.

‘Robust’ is the honest word. A central bank that justifies a move by its baseline is betting on its forecast. One that calls the move robust across scenarios is admitting it does not know which scenario it is in. That is less comfortable and more truthful. It also refused to promise anything: “The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path”1.

Hindsight. It did move again: a further 25 basis points on 10 September, to 2.50%, saying inflation “is set to remain well above target for an extended period”3. The projection for 2026 stayed at 3.0%; the one for 2027 rose to 2.5%3. For September, Eurostat’s final figure put euro-area inflation at 3.8%, with core at 2.5%4. For you, the lesson of June is a practical one: when a committee says it is acting on risks rather than on its central case, plan with the risks too.

item.title: Sixty days was the honest clause
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: A June memorandum promised safe passage through Hormuz, free of charge, for sixty days only. The price fell as if the strait had reopened. It had reopened on paper.
item.content:encoded:
A June memorandum promised safe passage through Hormuz, free of charge, for sixty days only. The price fell as if the strait had reopened. It had reopened on paper.

On 17 June President Trump and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding that declared the removal of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and committed Iran to “make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels with no charge, for 60 days only”1. The future administration of the strait was left to Iran, in consultation with Oman and other Gulf states1.

The screen believed it. On the EIA spot series Brent was $80.33 on the day of signing and $68.53 on 2 July, its lowest since early February3. That was a pre-war price for a strait that was not running at pre-war volumes. Under the agreement, traffic rose to an average of about 20 vessels a day: better than five, still only a fifth of normal2.

The water did not. On 25 June a ship was attacked in Omani waters, prompting US airstrikes; there were further attacks on ships off Oman on 7 and 8 July1. On 14 July the United States resumed its blockade, and traffic fell back to about five vessels a day2. Brent spot was $83.69 that day and $105.32 by 23 July3.

The honest clause. Read in hindsight, the memorandum told you its own limits. “Best efforts” is not a guarantee. “With no charge” implies that a charge was on the table. “For 60 days only” is a deadline, and deadlines in a corridor dispute are where the next negotiation starts, not where the last one ends. None of that required foresight; it required reading the clause with the number in it.

What it meant for you. A business that locked in fuel or freight at the early-July low would have done well for a fortnight. One that treated the low as the new normal would have had a hard August. The constructive habit is simple and unglamorous: when a price moves on a signature, check the traffic data before you check your budget. Ships are slower than headlines, and more honest.

item.title: Six months, five ships a day
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Half a year into the war, the strait carried a twentieth of its old traffic. The world adapted around it, by pipeline, by detour and by drawing down the cupboard. The cupboard was the part with a bottom.
item.content:encoded:
Half a year into the war, the strait carried a twentieth of its old traffic. The world adapted around it, by pipeline, by detour and by drawing down the cupboard. The cupboard was the part with a bottom.

By late August the war was six months old, and the Strait of Hormuz was, in Al Jazeera’s phrase, “in effect, closed”. From 15 July to 23 August an average of about five vessels a day passed through, a drop of almost 95% from pre-war traffic of about a hundred a day1. On 26 August Kpler counted ten visible commodity-vessel transits, below a 10-day average of about 152.

The world went round. Gulf crude exports had fallen by about 47%, from roughly 17 million barrels a day in 2025 to about 9 million in August, per Al Jazeera’s figures, and direct crude exports through the strait averaged 2.2 million barrels a day on Kpler data1. Saudi Arabia’s port calls fell by only about 15%, thanks to its pipelines and Red Sea ports; Kuwait, whose only sea route runs through the strait, saw port calls fall by 86%1. Geography, it turns out, is a balance sheet.

The price, by then, was not panicking. Brent spot was $90.18 on 27 August3, well below the April peak; Al Jazeera put oil about 20% above pre-war levels and quoted experts who called the rise “somewhat muted” because markets had proved “adaptive and resilient”1. That is the constructive reading, and it is true.

The other reading was in the same article. Richard Matthews of Gibson Shipbrokers explained that inventories had been building before the war and had cushioned the shock, and then added: “It’s only around now where we’ve kind of burnt through that buffer”1. Adaptation by detour can go on for a long time. Adaptation by drawing stocks has a bottom, and the bottom does not announce itself in advance.

Hindsight. Within three weeks of that interview, drones damaged the Saudi pipeline that bypasses the strait4, and the spot price was back above $1203. The adaptive system had been adaptive with a finite cupboard. For you, August is the month to remember the difference between resilience and reserve: the first is a skill, the second is a stock, and only the stock runs out.

item.title: The bypass breaks, both banks hike
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: In one week the pipeline that carried Saudi oil around Hormuz was hit, the ECB raised rates and the Fed did the same. The Fed decided on the very day the ECB's increase took effect. The tank had made the argument for both.
item.content:encoded:
In one week the pipeline that carried Saudi oil around Hormuz was hit, the ECB raised rates and the Fed did the same. The Fed decided on the very day the ECB's increase took effect. The tank had made the argument for both.

In the second week of September, drones launched from Iraq damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which can carry 7 million barrels a day from the Gulf to the Red Sea coast, and Riyadh shut it4. It was the main route by which Saudi crude avoided Hormuz. Kpler estimated the market could lose 120 million barrels if it stayed closed for a month4. Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates summed it up: “The longer the shutdown, the higher the price”4.

Two prices again. Brent futures settled at $105.68 on Monday 14 September, after nearly touching $1104. The EIA’s spot price for a physical North Sea barrel was $121.25 that day and $130.80 the next5. If you heat a building or run a fleet, the second number was yours.

Frankfurt had moved the same week. On 10 September the ECB raised its three key rates by 25 basis points, the deposit rate to 2.50% from 16 September, saying inflation “is set to remain well above target for an extended period”1. Its staff now projected inflation of 3.0% this year and 2.5% next, and it repeated that it was “not pre-committing to a particular rate path”1.

Washington followed, on the very day the ECB’s increase took effect. On 16 September the Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4%, by twelve votes to none, saying the move “will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”2. In July the same committee had held by nine votes to three, with three members already asking for this increase3. The dissent was the forecast; the September vote was the receipt.

What the chart says, and what it does not. It shows two central banks that spent 2024 and 2025 cutting, and 2026 reversing6,7. It does not show that they were wrong to cut; the energy shock that changed their minds began in February. Reading hindsight into a rate path is the easiest mistake in finance. The honest reading is narrower: when the price of energy is set by a corridor, policy is set by how long the corridor stays shut.

For you, the useful conclusion is the dull one. If your loan, your deposit or your rent is linked to either of these lines, the committees have told you plainly that they are watching the tank, not the screen, and that they will not promise the next step in advance.

item.title: Resilience is an inventory
item.dc:creator: Dr. Benjamin Koch
item.description: Six months after April's warning, the IMF's growth number had not moved and its inflation number had. The Fund's own explanation is a list of things that run down.
item.content:encoded:
Six months after April's warning, the IMF's growth number had not moved and its inflation number had. The Fund's own explanation is a list of things that run down.

On 13 October the IMF published its autumn World Economic Outlook, Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices2. The headline number was the same as in April: world growth of 3.1% in 20261,3. In the Fund’s words, the forecast “remains broadly unchanged from April, despite a more persistent energy market disruption than anticipated”1.

What did move. Headline inflation for 2026 was now forecast at 4.7%, against 4.4% in April, and at 4.1% for 2027, against 3.7%1,3. Core inflation was put at 3.9% this year1. Growth for 2027 was raised to 3.4%, from 3.2% in April1,3. Put simply: the world produced about what the Fund expected and paid more for it.

The explanation is a list. The IMF credited two sets of factors. The first: “the rerouting of energy supplies, increased energy production in other countries, inventory drawdowns, substitution to other sources of energy, including renewables, and higher energy efficiency”1. The second: an investment boom driven by artificial intelligence1. Read the first list slowly. Rerouting has a cost, production elsewhere has a ceiling, and inventory drawdowns have a floor.

The Fund said so itself. “Dwindling energy inventories could allow geopolitical shocks to transmit even more forcefully to energy prices,” the blog warned, and the investment boom was “concentrating risks”, making the expansion “heavily reliant on a small number of firms, sectors, and economies”1. Six days earlier the IEA had put the remaining public emergency stocks of its members at around 1.1 billion barrels4. That is a large cushion, and a smaller one than in March.

The constructive reading. The record of 2026 so far is not one of collapse. It is one of a system that bent: ships rerouted, producers elsewhere pumped, households and firms paid more and carried on. That is genuinely good news, and the desk is happy to say it. It is also news with a maturity date. Resilience built from stocks is a loan; resilience built from capacity is an asset. For the year’s last quarter, the question for you is which of the two your own budget is leaning on.
